review_basis: Read complete revision 4 specification, the six additional native-prepare/cache claims, and their definitions/proofs. Mechanically checked all 22 SQL obligation symbols/statements against spec/sql-types.json.
Inspected current revision 3 guard/protocol sources and preserved backup failure. Registered baseline_changes returned an empty list, so revision 4 production implementation has not begun.

Ran read-only grammar probes with the pinned workspace executable to check native statements, duplicate ordered statement families, wrapper forms, quoted/overlong names, comments and unsafe expressions.
Consulted official PostgreSQL 16 PREPARE, EXECUTE and lexical documentation for session-local statements, expression parameters, unquoted folding and identifier truncation.
approval_basis: Revision 4 replaces a blanket ban that blocked actual full pg_dump with a bounded shared-namespace admission rule. It preserves exact grammar acceptance of the complete client-issued source and requires a connection-local admitted target for SQL EXECUTE.
Sole top-level statements, conservative ASCII names of at most 63 bytes, unchanged nested-production/mode/function restrictions, bounded state and no direct fallback retain the established boundary.

The native PREPARE request includes its statically parsed body; no arbitrary executable string is admitted through Bind/COPY parameters. SQL EXECUTE parameter expressions themselves remain subject to the normal policy.

The six new abstract claims establish native execution admission/target provenance, missing-name denial, native-to-protocol binding, pure cache lookup and accepted witnesses without asserting backend execution or adapter correctness.
The revision 3 failure remains BLOCKED evidence. Revision 4 requires unmodified full pg_dump/pg_restore with ACLs rather than suppressing backup contents.
read_only_parser_probe_results: PREPARE getColumnACLs(pg_catalog.oid) AS SELECT $1 and EXECUTE getColumnACLs(42) are grammar accepted with exact returned source and single PrepareStmt/ExecuteStmt families.
EXECUTE s; EXECUTE s yields ordered families [ExecuteStmt, ExecuteStmt]; converting this list to a set would incorrectly erase the multi-statement evidence.

CREATE TEMP TABLE tmp AS EXECUTE s yields outer [ExecuteStmt] despite its leading CREATE token. A singleton family check alone is insufficient; require the correct leading PREPARE/EXECUTE token as well.
EXPLAIN EXECUTE s yields outer ExplainStmt and nested ExecuteStmt, so the nested production restriction remains necessary.
Unsafe set_config in PREPARE bodies and EXECUTE arguments is grammar accepted, confirming that existing policy checks must scan the complete native statement before forwarding.

Quoted names and 64-character ASCII names are grammar accepted and therefore need the independent conservative name policy. Leading comments are absent from the token list, which supports token-based classification without source-prefix guessing.
implementation_acceptance_notes: Keep statementFamilies as an ordered list with duplicates. Require exactly one expected family and the matching leading PREPARE/EXECUTE token, then apply every nested forbidden-production check; do not whitelist all ExecuteStmt productions globally.

Extract names from verified lexer tokens, require the specified ASCII pattern and byte length, and lowercase only native SQL identifiers. Protocol statement-name bytes remain exact: SQL EXECUTE Foo targets foo and must not accidentally match protocol name Foo.

Treat classification, native name extraction and PREPARE body span as explicit trusted adapter work. Do not infer grammar structure from a textual AS substring, a regex over comments/strings, or a substring-only Lean premise.

Cache only immutable grammar/policy classification. Every request, including a cache hit, must update or consult its own connection-local statement state; another connection or a pure cache lookup cannot create native preparation.

Handle native/protocol duplicate names, Close, backend Parse/PREPARE errors and pipelined requests conservatively. Optimistic accepted metadata must never be reported as successful backend preparation, and a parsed PREPARE utility wrapper must not be represented as already executed. Prefer rejecting ambiguous replacement rather than implying source identity for a backend object retained after failure.

Test both cross-protocol directions, native unknown names, case distinctions, 63/64-byte boundaries, quoted/Unicode names, cache hits on fresh connections, state exhaustion, unsafe body/argument set_config, EXPLAIN, CREATE TABLE AS EXECUTE and repeated-family multi-statements.

After the six approvals and two clean final proof builds, rerun the full wire/real PostgreSQL verifier with a daemon whose loaded-input hashes and pinned parser binary match the frozen sources. Run full native pg_dump/pg_restore with ACLs and preserve the independent revocation journal and existing corpus.
formal_limits: bodyPart proves only that a nonempty body string is a substring of the admitted PREPARE request. It does not establish that this substring is the grammar-selected query body; classification and span correctness remain trusted adapter assumptions.

NativeExecute assumes its request has been classified as EXECUTE and its supplied name has been normalized/extracted correctly. The formal theorem proves admitted-request/table-lookup facts from those premises, not SQL lexical correspondence.

The model still omits backend success, lifecycle/error correspondence, Python implementation refinement, wire framing, real cache/state behavior and network isolation. No stronger claim is warranted by the six additions.
No Lean build or PostgreSQL query execution was performed in this review. Final two-clean-build and implementation/runtime gates remain outstanding.
approval_scope: Exact revision 4 implementation design only. This approval does not establish completed backup recovery, adapter correctness, runtime conformance or rights beyond user-authorized local execution.
